features.title: Bringing the court day into one workflow.
features.intro: How interviews with lawyers shaped a product for finding and following court information.

blocks.title: Starting with the work people already do
paragraphs: CounselMate began with a workflow problem: lawyers were losing time moving between fragmented sources of court information.

I interviewed more than 30 lawyers in person to understand where that time went and which problems should shape the first version. The research gave me a basis for prioritizing a focused product, rather than starting with a long list of possible features.

blocks.title: Bringing the information together
paragraphs: The resulting app combines cause lists, live boards, case details, orders, judgments and real-time alerts in one workflow for Rajasthan High Court lawyers.

My work connected the research to the build: identifying the useful information, deciding which parts belonged in the MVP and bringing them together into a product people could use through the court day.

blocks.title: Looking at adoption and time saved
paragraphs: The résumé snapshot reports approximately 300 monthly active users and around 45 minutes saved per user per day. These are reported measures, not a guarantee of savings for every user.

The important product connection is between the original research and the result: the interviews identified time lost across fragmented sources, and the app addressed that fragmentation through one place to follow relevant information.

blocks.title: What the case study demonstrates
paragraphs: CounselMate connects customer discovery, MVP prioritization and hands-on execution. It is a practical example of the direction I want to take into product management: understand a specific workflow, choose the useful scope and build around the people doing the work.

features.title: When self-service needs a simpler starting point.
features.intro: How hospital feedback changed the way identity policies were configured.

blocks.title: The original approach
paragraphs: Hospital IT teams needed to configure identity and access policies for Oracle Health. An API-first setup gave technically equipped teams a flexible way to do that work.
But the pilot revealed a difference between customer groups. Smaller hospitals did not always have the IT capacity or policy expertise needed to use the full configuration surface.

blocks.title: Changing the starting point
paragraphs: I used that feedback to add default-policy workflows. The change gave smaller teams a simpler starting point while retaining the broader capability for organizations that needed it.

This was a product decision about how different users could reach a useful result. More configuration options were not the complete answer; the setup also needed to fit the capabilities of the team using it.

blocks.title: Following the result
paragraphs: The revised self-service workflow reached more than 17 hospitals, and onboarding support requests fell by 23%.
The story connects pilot learning to a change in the experience and then to an operational outcome. It is one of the clearest examples of how my engineering work has included product judgment.

features.title: Making room for the next live exam.
features.intro: Video, storage and messaging decisions behind a proctoring platform.

blocks.title: Reliability during a live event
paragraphs: An online assessment depends on the systems connecting candidates, proctors and administrators. My work at Mercer Mettl included changes to those systems as the platform supported large, time-sensitive sessions.
I rearchitected the WebRTC streaming server to handle 40,000 concurrent video requests. The résumé identifies University of São Paulo examinations as one of the high-volume contexts for that work.

blocks.title: Storage that could scale across servers
paragraphs: In a separate initiative, I led three engineers through a migration from EBS to EFS. Moving from server-bound storage to a shared file system allowed workloads to scale across servers during peak demand.
The migration reduced infrastructure costs by 43%, approximately ₹30 lakh. That result belongs to the storage initiative; it should not be attributed to the video-server redesign.

blocks.title: Evaluating the messaging layer
paragraphs: I also worked on migration from ActiveMQ to Amazon SQS FIFO, with message capacity moving from 200 to 1,000 messages per second.
The business case forecast ₹1.45 crore in annual savings; this is a projected benefit, not a claim of realized savings.

blocks.title: Connecting decisions to product operations
paragraphs: These projects sit at the intersection of engineering choices and product needs: continuity during exams, capacity for traffic spikes and the cost of operating the platform.
